text.p: Sprint Corp soundly beat Wall Street consensus estimates for its first quarter earnings on Tuesday, but share analysts said the reason was not a durable factor that will help the company in the future.
Sprint earnings per share were $0.67 per share, well above the $0.63 consensus forecast on First Call, but lower than the $0.78 posted a year ago.
"It was double-sided," said analyst Richard Klugman of Goldman Sachs. "It was a penny better than we forecast but they got to it via lower PCS dilution than expected," he said.
Personal Communication Services (PCS) is one of many components of Sprint's ambitious strategy to offer a bundle of communications products and services across the country.
Sprint said that the costs of paying for the wireless licenses and building the PCS network would pick up during the rest of the year.
Sprint shares were 7/8 higher at 44-5/8 at 1130 EDT/1615 GMT, in line with the firm broad market.
Analysts say that Sprint's stock price is driven by how well it executes that plan, which is aimed at tying in existing customers as much as winning new ones.
"Earnings are not driving the stock price," said Bette Massick, an analyst at Bear Stearns.
However, analysts agree the company is outperforming AT&T Corp and MCI Communications Corp in the key long distance market.
"Sprint's long distance business is growing the fastest of the big three," Massick said.
Analysts were sanguine abou the company's prospects overall, noting a good performance under trying circumstances when the long distance market is intensively competitive.
The company also seems to have recovered well from the loss to AT&T in 1996 of the huge contract to handle toll free calls to the Internal Revenue Service.
"I think this company will continue to gain market share across the board in long distance," said Klugman. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
